title: Ada Lovelace, the first programmer
text: Ada Lovelace, born in 1815, is now celebrated as a pioneer of computing, yet her {{1}} (CONTRIBUTE) was ignored for a century. Daughter of the poet Byron, she was educated in mathematics by her anxious mother, who hoped numbers would discourage any poetic {{2}} (INCLINE). When Ada met Charles Babbage, she was immediately fascinated by his design for a mechanical {{3}} (CALCULATE) engine. Her notes on the machine include what is now regarded as the first computer {{4}} (OPERATE) in history. More strikingly, she foresaw that such machines could manipulate any symbols, not just numbers — an idea of extraordinary {{5}} (DEEP). Babbage, ironically, showed less {{6}} (ENTHUSIASTIC) for this abstraction than she did. Ada died young, and her work sank into {{7}} (OBSCURE) until the twentieth century. Today, her notes are admired as a triumph of scientific {{8}} (IMAGINE).

gaps.explanation: 'calculating engine' — Babbage's machine was a calculating engine.
'computer operation' — the noun from operate; the notes describe operations.
'showed less enthusiasm' — the noun form here.
